query: Earlier automotive-catalyst research reported that Cu–Ni catalysts can oxidize CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures without platinum-group metals, while Pd–Cu and Pt–Cu catalysts can resist poisoning by H2O and NO and enable oxidation below 150 °C. Multi-principal-element catalysts in nearly equiatomic ratios have also been explored as a framework for combining high activity, thermal stability, and reduced platinum-group-metal use. These prior results demonstrate individual capabilities but do not establish the combined performance demanded by increasingly stringent regulations: clean exhaust during transient and low-temperature operation, resistance to relevant poisons, and durability over a vehicle lifetime despite the mileage-related degradation observed in real-driving-emission studies. Starting from a near-equiatomic, multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst, what single intervention could address this combined activity, poisoning-resistance, and lifetime-durability problem without sacrificing low platinum-group-metal use? State one hypothesis identifying the intervention, explaining how it would work, predicting the change relative to the unmodified catalyst, defining the exhaust and aging conditions over which it should apply, citing supporting prior evidence, and specifying an experiment whose result would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Depositing an ultrathin, conformal ceria (CeO2) overlayer on a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst will simultaneously improve low-temperature oxidation activity, resistance to poisoning by H2O and NO, and long-term durability, without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
generation.material_initial_state: A near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy catalyst (with elements such as Cu, Ni, Pd, Pt in nearly equiatomic ratios) prepared via conventional alloying and surface processing methods.
generation.intervention: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) of a 2–3 nm ceria overlayer onto the catalyst surface to create an active interface.
generation.conditions: Catalyst activity and stability are evaluated under simulated automotive exhaust conditions: transient and low-temperature operation with oxidations performed below 150 °C in an atmosphere containing CO, volatile hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO. Durability tests involve accelerated aging (thermal and chemical cycling) designed to mimic vehicle lifetime mileage.
generation.structural_mediator: The ceria overlayer forms active metal/oxide interfaces that provide oxygen storage capability and generate oxygen vacancies, which help promote oxidation reactions at lower temperatures while suppressing the adsorption of poisoning species.
generation.mechanism: Ceria’s oxygen storage and release capacity provides additional reactive oxygen species at the catalyst surface to facilitate oxidation of CO and hydrocarbons at lower temperatures. Its conformal coverage also acts as a physical barrier that minimizes the adsorption of poisoning molecules (like H2O and NO) on critical catalytic sites, and its thermal stability helps protect against sintering and deactivation during long-term exposure to harsh exhaust conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unmodified catalyst, the ceria-modified catalyst will exhibit lower light-off temperatures for oxidation reactions, enhanced tolerance to poisoning species, and improved long-term durability as measured by maintained activity after accelerated aging.
generation.baseline: The unmodified near-equiatomic multi-principal-element catalyst known to exhibit degradation under combined low-temperature and poisoning conditions over simulated extended automotive use.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits should hold under exhaust conditions below 150 °C with the specified gas mixtures and aging treatments. Uncertainty remains regarding potential overlayer instability (e.g., de-wetting or sintering) under extreme cycling conditions, which would limit performance benefits.
generation.uncertainty: While ceria overlayers are known to enhance oxidation catalysis and durability in related systems, the integration with multi-principal-element alloys in nearly equiatomic compositions is less explored. Variability in ALD process parameters and interfacial stability under prolonged cycling could affect the outcome.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst samples using the same near-equiatomic multi-principal-element alloy synthesis: one sample receives an ALD-deposited 2–3 nm ceria overlayer, and the control remains unmodified. Expose both samples to simulated automotive exhaust environments containing CO, volatile hydrocarbons, H2O, and NO at temperatures below 150 °C. Perform light-off tests (measuring temperature for 50% conversion) and accelerated aging (thermal cycling and poisoning gas exposure mimicking vehicle mileage) over a designated period.
measurements: Light-off temperature for oxidation of CO and select hydrocarbons
Catalytic conversion efficiency at set temperatures below 150 °C
Surface characterization (e.g., TEM, XPS) to assess overlayer integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ceria-modified catalyst does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >10 °C lower light-off temperature, higher conversion efficiency, and improved retention of catalytic activity post-aging) compared to the unmodified catalyst, then the hypothesis that ALD-deposited ceria improves combined activity, poisoning resistance, and durability is falsified.
